title: CH-302: Carbonyl Reactions & Mechanisms
description: This deck covers fundamental principles of carbonyl addition reactions, including the electrophilic nature of carbonyl carbons, the formation of tetrahedral intermediates, Grignard reagent reactions, and acid-catalyzed hydration processes.
subject: Organic Chemistry

cards.front: What is the primary electronic characteristic of a carbonyl carbon?
cards.back: The carbonyl carbon possesses a partial positive charge, making it an electrophilic site prone to nucleophilic attack.
cards.sourceEvidence: Carbonyl carbon has partial positive charge (electrophilic site)
cards.verifiedFactCheck: Carbonyl groups are polarized due to the electronegativity of oxygen, creating a delta-positive carbon center.

cards.front: Describe the hybridization change during nucleophilic attack on a carbonyl carbon.
cards.back: The carbon atom transitions from sp2 hybridization (trigonal planar) to sp3 hybridization (tetrahedral intermediate).
cards.sourceEvidence: Nucleophile attacks sp2 carbon forming tetrahedral intermediate (sp3)
cards.mnemonic: 2-3-Tetra: sp2 to sp3 in a Tetrahedron.
cards.verifiedFactCheck: Standard mechanism for nucleophilic acyl addition where nucleophile geometry shifts to accommodate bonding.

cards.front: What is the general product of a reaction between an aldehyde and a Grignard reagent?
cards.back: The reaction produces a secondary alcohol (after acidic workup).
cards.sourceEvidence: Grignard Reagents (R-MgX) add alkyl groups to aldehydes to yield 2° alcohols
cards.verifiedFactCheck: Grignard reagents are strong nucleophiles that add to carbonyls; formal dehydration/workup leads to secondary alcohols.

cards.front: What is the product of acid-catalyzed hydration of a carbonyl?
cards.back: Acid-catalyzed hydration forms geminal diols (also known as hydrates).
cards.sourceEvidence: Acid-catalyzed hydration forms geminal diols reversibly
cards.verifiedFactCheck: Hydration of aldehydes/ketones in acid creates a species with two hydroxyl groups on the same carbon (gem-diol).

cards.front: What is the standard workup step following the addition of a Grignard reagent to a carbonyl?
cards.back: The intermediate is treated with H3O+ (acidic workup) to protonate the alkoxide and produce the final alcohol.
cards.verifiedFactCheck: Grignard additions require a proton source (acidic workup) to convert the resulting magnesium alkoxide to the alcohol.

title: Cardiovascular Physiology & Hemodynamics
description: Detailed flashcards generated from Module 4 lecture notes covering the cardiac cycle, pressures, and volumes.
subject: Biology & Medicine

cards.front: What mechanical event defines the isovolumetric ventricular contraction phase?
cards.back: Both the atrioventricular (mitral/tricuspid) and semilunar (aortic/pulmonary) valves are closed, causing ventricular pressure to rise rapidly with no change in ventricular volume.
cards.mnemonic: ISO = same, VOLUME = size. Doors locked, pressure rocks!
cards.sourceEvidence: Scanned Note: "AV and semilunar valves both closed; ventricular pressure rises steeply."
cards.verifiedFactCheck: Verified against Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (14th Ed., Chapter 9).

cards.front: How is Cardiac Output (CO) mathematically determined from Stroke Volume and Heart Rate?
cards.back: CO = Heart Rate (HR, bpm) × Stroke Volume (SV, mL/beat). Typical resting output is ~5 L/min in a healthy adult.
cards.sourceEvidence: Scanned Formula Box: "CO = Heart Rate x Stroke Volume | EF = (SV / EDV) * 100%"
cards.verifiedFactCheck: 100% textbook canon in human cardiovascular physiology.

cards.front: State the Frank-Starling Law of the heart and its physiological significance.
cards.back: The force of cardiac contraction is directly proportional to the initial muscle fiber length (end-diastolic volume/preload). Increased preload leads to increased stroke volume, ensuring output matches venous return.
cards.sourceEvidence: Scanned Note: "Increased preload leads to increased stroke volume"
cards.verifiedFactCheck: Grounded in actin-myosin filament overlap optimization within sarcomeres up to physiological limits.

cards.front: What is the formula for Ejection Fraction (EF) and what is considered normal?
cards.back: EF = (Stroke Volume / End-Diastolic Volume) × 100%. A normal resting value is between 55% and 70%. Below 40% indicates systolic heart failure.
cards.sourceEvidence: Scanned Diagram bottom equation: "EF = (SV / EDV) x 100%"
cards.verifiedFactCheck: Corresponds with American College of Cardiology (ACC/AHA) diagnostic criteria.

title: Organic Chemistry: Carbonyl Addition Mechanisms
description: Reaction pathways, electrophilic carbonyl reactivity, Grignard additions, and hydrate equilibria.
subject: Chemistry

cards.front: Why is the carbonyl carbon strongly electrophilic compared to alkene carbons?
cards.back: The high electronegativity difference between carbon (2.5) and oxygen (3.5) polarizes the C=O double bond, placing a significant partial positive charge (δ+) on the carbonyl carbon.
cards.sourceEvidence: Scanned Note: "Carbonyl carbon has partial positive charge (electrophilic site)"
cards.verifiedFactCheck: Direct resonance contributor: C=O <-> C(+)-O(-). Solid organic chemistry canon.

cards.front: What product is formed when an aldehyde is treated with a Grignard reagent (R-MgX) followed by aqueous acid workup?
cards.back: A secondary (2°) alcohol is formed. (Formaldehyde yields a 1° alcohol; ketones yield a 3° alcohol).
cards.verifiedFactCheck: Nucleophilic carbanion equivalent attack followed by hydronium protonation.

cards.front: What geometry change occurs at the carbonyl carbon upon nucleophilic attack?
cards.back: The carbon changes from sp² hybridized trigonal planar (120° bond angles) to sp³ hybridized tetrahedral intermediate (~109.5° bond angles).
cards.sourceEvidence: Scanned Note: "Nucleophile attacks sp2 carbon forming tetrahedral intermediate (sp3)"
cards.verifiedFactCheck: Standard Bürgi-Dunitz angle trajectory (~107°) leading to sp3 intermediate.

title: Calculus: Fundamental Theorems & Series
description: Calculus theorems, derivative-integral relationships, integration techniques, and convergence tests.
subject: Mathematics

cards.front: What is the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Part 1)?
cards.back: If f is continuous on [a, b], then the function g(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt is continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), and g'(x) = f(x).
cards.sourceEvidence: Scanned Note: "FTC 1: d/dx [integral from a to x of f(t) dt] = f(x)"
cards.verifiedFactCheck: Rigorous statement per Stewart Calculus 9th Edition.

cards.front: State the Integration by Parts formula and its origin.
cards.back: ∫ u dv = u·v - ∫ v du. It is derived directly from the Product Rule for differentiation: d/dx [u·v] = u'·v + u·v'.
cards.sourceEvidence: Scanned Box: "int(u dv) = uv - int(v du)"
